title: Submarine Power and Communication Cables
analyses: Axial tension, bending and torsion analysis
Cable fatigue and cyclic loading analysis
Cable touchdown and seabed interaction analysis
Thermal rating and heat dissipation analysis
Mechanical crushing and external pressure analysis
Extreme storm and vessel-motion response analysis

models.text: The suite should implement elastic rod theory, Euler–Bernoulli and Timoshenko beam formulations, nonlinear catenary equations, Cosserat rod theory, axial tension–bending–torsion relationships, geometric nonlinear finite elements, seabed contact mechanics, frictional sliding and cable instability models.

The suite should incorporate Ohm's law, Kirchhoff's current and voltage laws, Maxwell's equations, Gauss's law, Faraday's law, Ampère–Maxwell law, electromagnetic constitutive relationships, skin-effect models, proximity-effect models, conductor resistance, inductance, capacitance, dielectric loss and electromagnetic field diffusion.

It should include IEC 60287 current-rating methods, IEC 60853 cyclic and emergency thermal rating models, IEC 60909 short-circuit calculation methods where relevant, AC transmission-line models, distributed parameter cable models, sheath and armour loss models, dielectric heating, electrical insulation stress and short-circuit thermal withstand calculations.

The suite should implement Fourier heat conduction, transient heat diffusion, heat capacity models, thermal resistance networks, soil thermal conductivity relationships, Joule heating, coupled electrothermal modelling, seabed thermal response and temperature-dependent conductor resistivity.

Optical communication modelling should include Maxwell-based wave propagation, optical waveguide mode theory, refractive-index profile models, attenuation relationships, Rayleigh scattering loss, chromatic dispersion, polarization-mode dispersion, optical link budget models, splice loss and optical fibre bend-loss models.

The suite should include Morison hydrodynamic loading, vessel motion analysis, wave-current interactions, dynamic cable tension, catenary laying, bend radius models, soil contact, cable burial resistance, jetting and trenching models, and scour-related seabed exposure.

These calculations should use S–N curves, Miner damage, strain-based fatigue, armour-wire fatigue, insulation ageing models, Weibull reliability distributions, fault-tree analysis, failure mode and effects analysis, probabilistic cable damage rates and risk-based cable protection methods.

The suite should integrate electrical–thermal–mechanical modelling, electromagnetic finite elements with heat-transfer simulation, dynamic cable mechanics with fatigue analysis, seabed thermal fields with electrical ampacity, nonlinear burial mechanics with cable integrity, and sensor-based thermal monitoring with numerical prediction.

inputs.text: Route coordinates, seabed bathymetry, cable length, water depth, slope, crossings and planned burial depth.
Conductor diameter, conductor area, insulation thickness, metallic sheath, screening layers, armour dimensions and overall cable diameter.
Conductor resistivity, temperature coefficient of resistance, dielectric permittivity, dielectric loss factor and insulation electrical strength.
Cable axial stiffness, bending stiffness, torsional stiffness, density, ultimate tensile strength and fatigue characteristics.
Rated voltage, maximum operating voltage, AC frequency, current demand, power factor, transmitted power and load profiles.
Seabed temperature, soil thermal resistivity, seawater temperature, conductor thermal limits and insulation thermal properties.
Lay vessel configuration, cable installation tension, chute diameter, bending radii, deployment speed and laying sequence.
Trenching depth, trench width, soil properties, jetting capability, burial tool characteristics and backfill thermal properties.
Wave statistics, currents, water depth, seabed mobility, tidal variation and storm conditions.
Floating-platform motion, dynamic cable geometry, buoyancy elements, hang-off geometry and seabed touchdown conditions.
Pipeline crossing positions, neighbouring electrical circuits, cable spacing, fishing exposure and anchor interaction scenarios.
Maximum installation tension, minimum bend radius, allowable strain, crushing resistance and permissible fatigue damage.
Historical failures, joint properties, insulation defects, cable repair records and environmental damage exposure.

Fibre attenuation coefficients, optical wavelength, dispersion properties, splice losses, connector losses and optical transmitter/receiver characteristics where communication performance is modelled.

subtitle: Subsea power transmission, telecommunications cables, thermal rating, cable burial, electrical performance and dynamic mechanical integrity.
ic: The initial conditions shall define the installed or installation-stage cable route, including cable geometry, seabed contact, burial depth, crossings, free spans and dynamic cable configurations where applicable.

The mechanical starting state shall include cable pretension, bending curvature, residual installation stresses and the initial equilibrium under submerged weight and seabed support. Dynamic cables shall also have specified initial velocities, platform positions and touchdown conditions.

Thermal analyses shall initialize conductor, insulation, sheath, armour and surrounding soil or seawater temperatures. Electrical analyses shall establish the initial energized or de-energized operating condition, including conductor currents, voltages and relevant electrical states.

Cable burial studies shall define the initial trench geometry, sediment state, backfill characteristics and local seabed temperature distribution. Fatigue and degradation analyses shall initialize the cable's existing structural condition, damage state and available inspection information.
For communication cables, the initial optical operating conditions shall identify signal wavelengths, launched optical power and any active transmission conditions relevant to the model.
bc: Mechanical boundaries shall restrain or connect cable terminations to offshore structures, onshore landfalls, junction boxes and other equipment. Dynamic cable hang-off boundaries shall follow the motion of their supporting platform.

Cable–seabed boundaries shall represent contact pressure, friction, possible penetration, burial restraint and seabed thermal interaction. At crossings, contact or support constraints shall reflect the crossing protection arrangement.

Electrical boundaries shall prescribe appropriate sending-end voltage, current or power conditions and receiving-end load characteristics. Cable grounding and bonding shall be represented at sheaths, screens and armour where relevant.

Thermal boundaries shall represent conductive heat transfer into seabed soil, convective heat exchange with seawater and appropriate conditions at cable joints and terminations. Electromagnetic analyses shall use insulation-interface continuity and suitable external-field conditions.

For installation, the cable shall be subjected to prescribed lay tension, vessel motion, chute curvature, burial tool interaction and touchdown contact. Communication performance models shall prescribe optical transmitter conditions, receiver requirements and splice or termination losses.

calibration: Calibration should use cable manufacturer qualification tests, conductor resistance measurements, insulation tests, thermal experiments, mechanical fatigue tests and field cable monitoring.
Cable axial, bending and torsional stiffness should be calibrated using laboratory mechanical tests on representative complete cable constructions.
Thermal properties should be calibrated using measured conductor temperature, heating cycles, cable thermal resistance and seabed thermal resistivity measurements.
Electrical resistance, dielectric losses, sheath losses and armour losses should be informed by certified material measurements and electrical cable tests.
Electromagnetic response should be calibrated using controlled current-injection experiments and measured induced currents where applicable.
Cable–seabed contact and burial resistance should be calibrated using geotechnical tests, trenching trials, jetting experiments and actual installation records.
Dynamic cable hydrodynamic coefficients should be calibrated using oscillatory flow tests and measured suspended cable movement.
Crushing and external pressure models should use laboratory compression, pressure and mechanical damage tests.
Fatigue parameters should be calibrated using cyclic tension, bending and torsion experiments.
For communication cables, attenuation and dispersion parameters should be calibrated using optical measurements, splice tests and transmission system qualification data.
verification: Mechanical cable formulations should be verified against analytical suspended cable, tensioned beam and bending benchmarks.
Dynamic response should undergo time-step convergence, cable element refinement and sensitivity testing for stiffness and hydrodynamic loading.
Electrical calculations should be checked against independently calculated reference circuits and cable electrical property benchmarks.
Thermal calculations should be verified using known steady and transient heat-transfer reference problems.
Electromagnetic models should be checked against canonical conductor configurations with independently established fields and induced-current behaviour.
Coupled electrical–thermal calculations should be tested for consistent conversion of electrical losses into thermal loads.
Cable burial and seabed contact models should be checked against known penetration, friction and soil resistance benchmarks.
Fatigue accumulation calculations should be verified using prescribed loading histories and known reference outcomes.
Communication calculations should be tested using prescribed optical attenuation, dispersion and component-loss cases.
validation: Static and dynamic cable response should be compared with independent laboratory tests and instrumented cable installations.
Cable operating temperatures and current ratings should be validated using thermal loading tests and independently monitored cable systems.
Electrical losses, impedance characteristics and induced currents should be assessed using controlled electrical experiments.
Seabed burial predictions should be compared with actual trenching and jetting records, burial depth surveys and measured soil conditions.
Cable free-span behaviour and fatigue predictions should be evaluated against representative dynamic test data.
Mechanical crushing and external pressure resistance should be assessed using independent structural qualification tests.
Optical communication performance should be compared with measured attenuation, dispersion and receiver performance over representative cable lengths.
Long-term reliability predictions should be assessed against inspection histories, cable fault records and independent operating experience.

geometry.text: Submarine electrical power cables, submarine communication cables, dynamic export cables, inter-array cables, optical fibre cables, armoured cables, subsea joints, cable terminations, burial trenches and cable protection systems.

geometry.cat: Conventional and universal CAD geometry formats
geometry.text: STEP, IGES, Parasolid, ACIS, DXF and supported DWG should be accepted for cable cross-sections, conductor geometry, insulation layers, metallic sheaths, armour layers, connectors, joints, protection structures and mechanical terminations.

DXF, SVG, STEP, IGES and structured CSV, JSON or XML descriptions should be supported for conductor shapes, insulation boundaries, metallic screens, armour wire positions, phase arrangements and cross-sectional layer properties. CAD-derived conductor and insulation domains should remain distinguishable for electrical, electromagnetic and thermal modelling.

CSV, TSV, XYZ, GeoJSON, GML, GeoPackage, Shapefile, LandXML, DXF three-dimensional polylines and documented JSON/XML route descriptions should be accepted for cable coordinates, seabed alignment, burial depth, crossings and three-dimensional dynamic cable configurations.

Nastran BDF, Abaqus INP, ANSYS CDB, Gmsh MSH, MED, UNV, VTK/VTU, Exodus and CGNS should be accepted where the receiving solver supports the corresponding mechanical, thermal, electrical or electromagnetic discretization. Geometry imported for electromagnetic and thermal calculations must retain the material regions and conductor interfaces relevant to the physical model.

STL, OBJ, PLY, GLB, LAS/LAZ, E57, GeoTIFF, ESRI ASCII Grid, XYZ bathymetry and suitable gridded sediment surfaces should be supported for cable-burial corridors, trench geometry, cable exposure, seabed irregularities and cable-crossing arrangements.
